transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is… it’s this memorial I’m putting together for my brother. It started out as a simple thing, you know, just honoring him properly, but it’s gotten much bigger than I meant it to. I’ve been spending most days on it now—chasing down songs he liked, calling people, figuring out displays, thinking about trips and who should be there and what needs to be shown.

My wife says I’ve let everything else slide. The garden, my walking group, regular things I used to keep up with… she says I’ve pushed just about all of it aside. I don’t know, to me it feels important, like if I don’t keep at it, it won’t be done right. But it’s taken over more than I expected, and that’s why I’m here.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried when you’re not working on the memorial, like your mind keeps going back to it even when you want to focus on other things?

Yes… yes, that’s a fair way to put it. It’s not always worry like, you know, sitting there trembling, but my mind just will not stay put when I’m not working on it. I can be trying to do something ordinary, and then suddenly I’m thinking, “No, the display case should have the old photograph on the left,” and before I can even finish that thought I’m off thinking about whether I need to take a road trip to find some cousin who might remember a song he used to sing, and then right after that a line from a ballad pops in my head and I’m trying to remember the next verse.

It jumps around like that. One idea after another, and they all feel important in the moment. I’ll think I should write it down, make a proper list, but by the time I get paper or sit at the table, there are already three or four more things crowding in. I can’t seem to slow it down enough to put it in any sensible order. So even when I’m not actively doing the memorial, my head is still running through it.
Have you noticed any periods where you felt unusually upbeat, energized, or more confident than usual while working on the memorial?

Yes, I have. I mean, I wouldn’t have called it “upbeat” at first, exactly, but there are times when I feel… lit up, I guess. Like suddenly everything about the memorial makes perfect sense, and I can see it all in my head—the photos, the songs, the people who need to hear it—and I feel full of purpose. Like this isn’t just some family thing, you know, it’s like the whole town is finally going to understand who my brother was and what our family meant.

And when I get that feeling, I do feel more confident. Maybe too confident, my wife would say. I’ll think, “No, this is exactly right, I know how it has to be,” and then if she asks whether we need all of it, or someone at the senior center says maybe the display is too much or they can’t help right then, I can snap. I don’t always mean to, but it comes out sharp, like they’re getting in the way of something important. One minute I’m inspired, like I’ve got this big clear mission, and the next I’m irritated because someone is slowing me down or questioning it.
Have there been times when you felt like you didn’t need as much sleep as usual, or that your thoughts were racing so much that it was hard to slow them down, even outside of working on the memorial?

Yes, the racing thoughts part, definitely. I don’t know that I always notice it right away, because in the moment it feels like I’m just trying to keep up with what needs doing, but then I realize my mind is jumping all over the place.

It’ll be like, one minute I’m thinking about the display case—where a photograph should go, whether it should be on the left or centered—and before I’ve even finished that, I’m thinking I ought to take a road trip to find a cousin who might remember something about my brother. Then right on top of that, some old ballad comes into my head, just one verse, and I’m trying to catch the next line before it disappears. And then there’s another thought after that.

It’s hard to slow it down enough to make any kind of proper list. I’ll sit there meaning to write things in order, but by the time I get the pen, there are already several more ideas crowding in. So yes, my thoughts do race like that. It’s not just one worry—it’s like a whole string of ideas pulling me along.

Have there been times when you felt so full of energy or ideas that you didn't feel like you needed much sleep at all, and it seemed like your thoughts were going so fast you couldn't even keep track of them?

Yes… I mean, the part about my thoughts going too fast, yes, very much. I know I’ve said something like this already, but that really is how it feels. My mind doesn’t just stay on one thing long enough for me to finish it. It jumps.

Like I’ll be thinking about the display case, just something simple like where one photograph ought to go, and before I’ve even settled that in my head, I’m already thinking maybe I need to go find a cousin who might remember some story or song. Then almost immediately some old ballad will come into my head—just a line or a verse—and I’m trying to grab hold of the next part before it slips away. And by then I’ve lost the first thought, or there are three more stacked on top of it.

That’s the frustrating thing. It all feels connected and important while it’s happening, but I can’t slow it down enough to put it in order. I’ll think, “All right, sit down, write a list,” but by the time I get a pen or get myself settled, the list has already changed in my head. It’s like I’m trying to take dictation from my own mind, but it’s talking faster than I can write.

Have you had any week or more where you felt unusually high, extremely confident, or irritable most of the day, nearly every day—not just while working on the memorial or interacting with others about it?

Yes… I think so. It’s hard for me to separate it from the memorial because that’s been the main thing everything seems to circle around, but it doesn’t always stay neatly in that box. There have been stretches where, most of the day, I feel like I’m just… charged up. Like I’m lit from the inside, full of purpose, like I can see exactly what needs to happen and everyone else is finally going to understand what our family meant.

And then if someone doesn’t go along with it—my wife asking if I’m making too much of the display, or someone at the senior center saying they can’t help right then—I can get sharp, really sharp. I’ll feel absolutely certain I’m right, and then I snap because it feels like they’re slowing down something important. It’s not just a little irritation in the moment; it can feel like I’m carrying that confidence and impatience around with me most of the day.
